title: Puppy Vaccination Schedule: What to Expect in the First Year
description: When puppies get their first vaccines, what each visit covers in the US and UK, and what to do before the course is finished.

quick: Puppy vaccines usually start at 6 to 8 weeks, with more doses every few weeks until about 16 to 18 weeks, then boosters. In the UK, PDSA says most puppies have 2 injections 2 to 4 weeks apart and are fully protected 2 to 4 weeks after the last one. Your vet sets the exact schedule, because it depends on where you live and your puppy's risks.

faq.q: When should a puppy get its first vaccine?
faq.a: The American Kennel Club lists distemper and parvovirus at 6 to 8 weeks as a general guideline, and PDSA says puppies should ideally start at around 6 to 8 weeks. The Kennel Club says most puppies receive their first set at around 8 weeks, depending on the vet's advice and whether the mother was fully vaccinated.

faq.q: Can I take my puppy outside before the vaccines are finished?
faq.a: PDSA advises that a puppy who has not finished the primary course should not be put on the ground in public places. You can carry them out, but do not let them meet unvaccinated dogs. Your garden is fine if no unvaccinated dogs have visited recently and it is secure. Ask your vet when it is safe to start walks.

faq.q: How many puppy vaccines are there?
faq.a: It depends on the country and the vet. The AKC lists several visits in the first year, including DHPP and rabies, plus optional vaccines for lifestyle. In the UK, PDSA says 2 injections are common and some puppies need a third.

faq.q: How much do puppy vaccines cost?
faq.a: Prices vary by country, clinic and package, and the AKC says that location is a big factor. Ask your vet for a written estimate for the whole puppy course so there are no surprises.

faq.q: Are there side effects after puppy vaccines?
faq.a: PDSA says side effects are rare and usually mild, for example a high temperature, low energy or reduced appetite, passing within 24 to 48 hours. Contact your vet if you see anything more serious.

faq.q: What happens if my puppy misses a vaccine?
faq.a: PDSA says dogs that have missed a booster may stay protected for 2 to 3 months after the due date and then are at risk again. Call your vet as soon as you realise, and ask what to do for a puppy that has not finished the primary course.

html:
You bring your puppy home and, within days, the vet asks which vaccine visits to book. It can feel like a lot of acronyms. The idea is simple, though: young puppies get a short series of vaccines, because protection from their mother fades while their own immunity is still building. Your vet will set the exact timing for your puppy, and this guide explains the usual pattern.

This article is general information, not veterinary advice. Rules for rabies and other vaccines differ by country and even by region, so use it to prepare your questions.

A general puppy vaccination timeline

The American Kennel Club is clear that there is not one schedule for every dog. Where you live and your puppy's risk factors matter, and some dogs do not need every vaccine. With that in mind, this is its general guideline for the first year in the US.

Puppy ageUsually recommendedOptional, by lifestyle
6 to 8 weeksDistemper, parvovirusBordetella
10 to 12 weeksDHPP (distemper, adenovirus or hepatitis, parainfluenza, parvovirus)Influenza, leptospirosis, bordetella, Lyme disease
16 to 18 weeksDHPP, rabiesInfluenza, Lyme disease, leptospirosis, bordetella
12 to 16 monthsDHPP, rabiesCoronavirus, leptospirosis, bordetella, Lyme disease

After the first year, the AKC lists DHPP boosters every 1 to 2 years and rabies every 1 to 3 years, as required by law. It also notes that heartworm has no vaccine, and that around 12 to 16 weeks it is worth talking to your vet about preventive medication.

What it looks like in the UK

PDSA says all dogs in the UK should be vaccinated against parvovirus, distemper, leptospirosis and infectious hepatitis, and that, depending on lifestyle, a dog may also need kennel cough and rabies vaccines. Puppies should ideally start at around 6 to 8 weeks old, with 2 injections 2 to 4 weeks apart, and they are fully protected 2 to 4 weeks after the final injection. Some puppies need a third injection as part of the primary course. Boosters follow, with leptospirosis every year and the others usually every three years.

The Kennel Club adds that puppies often get the first jabs from the breeder and the second with the new owner, and that breeders should pass on vaccination certificates. Take any paperwork to your first vet visit.

What do puppy vaccines protect against?

It helps to know what the acronyms stand for. According to PDSA, the core UK vaccines protect against four diseases. Parvovirus is highly contagious and potentially deadly, causing severe vomiting and diarrhoea. Distemper is very serious and often fatal, affecting the gut, heart, immune system, lungs, brain and nerves. Infectious hepatitis attacks the liver, kidneys, eyes and blood vessels, and the virus can survive in the environment for up to a year. The fourth is leptospirosis. The AKC's list also includes bordetella, the main cause of kennel cough, which is given as an injection or a nasal spray and is worth discussing if you plan to board your puppy.

Are puppy vaccine side effects common?

PDSA says side effects are rare and most dogs have none. If they happen they are likely to be mild, such as a high temperature, low energy or reduced appetite, and they pass within 24 to 48 hours. Serious side effects are extremely rare, but if you see any, speak to your vet. PDSA also points out that the risk from a vaccine is much lower than the risk of staying unvaccinated.

What if a vaccine is late or missed?

Do not wait for the next convenient date. PDSA explains that a dog who has been vaccinated before but missed a booster might have protection for 2 to 3 months after the booster was due, and after that is at risk again. If your puppy has only had part of the primary course, PDSA treats them as unvaccinated for safety purposes, so follow the same precautions and call your vet to rebook.

How do I socialise my puppy while waiting for full protection?

PDSA recommends asking your vet when your puppy will be protected, and not to take them to certain places or let them mix with unvaccinated dogs until then. It also says that puppies still need new experiences as soon as possible, so you can start in a garden that unvaccinated dogs do not use, carry your puppy when you are out so they can meet people and see new places, and let them meet fully vaccinated older dogs. Your vet can tell you what is safe in your area. Our socialization checklist shows how to do it in small, positive steps.

Before the course is finished

This is the part new owners worry about, because socialisation is time sensitive. PDSA advises that if your puppy has not finished the primary course, you should not put them on the ground in public places, although you can take them out if you carry them. They should not mix with unvaccinated dogs from outside your household, and you should not bring unknown dogs into your home. The garden is fine if no unvaccinated dogs have visited recently and it is secure.

That does not mean waiting. You can still introduce sights, sounds and gentle handling at home, and your vet can tell you how to do it safely. Our puppy socialization checklist has ideas that work before the first walks.

What to bring and ask at the appointment

  • Any vaccination certificates and health records from the breeder or rescue.
  • A list of questions: which vaccines your puppy needs where you live, what is optional, when to start walks, and when to start parasite prevention.
  • A towel or blanket, treats, and a carrier or a leash and harness, so the visit is calm and positive.

If you notice anything that worries you after a vaccine, such as swelling, vomiting or breathing problems, contact your vet or an emergency clinic straight away.

Keep a simple record

Write down each date, vaccine and the due date for the next visit, and put it in your phone calendar with a reminder. A missed dose can leave gaps, and PDSA warns that dogs who do not get all their vaccinations are at risk of catching infectious diseases. Also add these dates to your first week plan so the vet visit does not get lost.

Boosters and the second year

Vaccines do not end with the puppy course. PDSA explains that dogs need regular boosters throughout life: leptospirosis every year, and parvovirus, distemper and hepatitis usually every three years after the initial course. The AKC's general guideline lists a DHPP booster every 1 to 2 years and rabies every 1 to 3 years where the law requires it. Your vet will decide what is right, based on the vaccine used and your dog's lifestyle.

Lifestyle matters. PDSA says a kennel cough vaccine is usually needed if a dog spends time in kennels or doggy day care, has a dog walker, or attends dog events and shows, and that rabies vaccination is necessary for dogs that travel in and out of the UK. If you plan boarding, daycare or travel, tell your vet early so the timing works.

What about the cost?

The AKC notes that cost depends on several factors, with location a big one, and that urban vets often charge more than rural ones. It also says some municipal governments sponsor low-cost clinics for rabies vaccines. Ask your vet for a written estimate for the whole puppy course, including boosters and any optional vaccines, so you can plan ahead.
